boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Poison Spring record (April 18, 1864) in the Camden Expedition [April 1864]. The April 17 departure of the forage train and the capture of the steamer Homer are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, foraging and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Brigade (1,100 men) [US] and Marmaduke's and Maxey's Divisions [CS], and the frozen US bound is 1,100; the live field reads 1100 (US 1100; CS 0). Britton says the escort was 695 men, joined on the road by Duncan's 383 infantry, 90 cavalry and two howitzers, and that the Confederate force was thirty-seven hundred picked men and twelve guns from Marmaduke's, Cabell's and Maxey's divisions. Price says the train was guarded by about 1,500 men and four guns.
claims.rationale: Escort components, an interested estimate and a retrospective count of the attackers; the frozen and live US 1,100 has no inspected basis, the Confederate divisions are named differently, and Britton's components are not summed here. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live CS zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Britton says the high ground was covered with pine timber that limited sight to about a hundred yards and hid the Union line from the Confederate artillery, that the fight turned on a field of twenty to thirty acres, and that the retreat crossed timber, brush and ravines where the guns had to be abandoned. NPS says Williams's men regrouped in a marsh to the north. Price names the site on the Washington, Munn's Mill and Camden road.
claims.rationale: Ground described by a history, a summary and an interested report; no map verification.

claims.rationale: Supply statements with differing wagon counts; no quartermaster return inspected.

claims.value: Britton says Maxey, the senior of three brigadier generals, commanded the combined force and ordered Greene's brigade into the centre, and that Thayer detailed Williams to command the escort; Price also names Maxey as commanding. Price reported Williams killed; an editorial footnote calls this a mistake. The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals John S. Marmaduke and Samuel Bell Maxey and Colonel James M. Williams; the live page lists Marmaduke without rank and Williams.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a history and an interested report; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and Price's report of Williams's death is preserved as an error flagged by the compiler.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 415 total (US 301; CS 114), and the live field agrees. Britton gives the Union loss as 122 killed, 97 wounded and 81 missing, with the First Kansas Colored Infantry losing 117 killed and 65 wounded; Maxey's incomplete returns as 17 killed and 88 wounded; and only 4 Black soldiers reported captured. He says Confederate troops shot wounded Black soldiers on the field and that Cabell reported one regiment killed at least 80. Price claims near 500 Union dead, mostly Black soldiers.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The killing of wounded and captured Black soldiers means Union killed and missing figures are not ordinary combat categories.

open_questions: Williams's report and the other Union reports on Poison Spring (Nos. 24-33), Maxey's, De Morse's and Tandy Walker's reports (Nos. 75-77), Cabell's and Crawford's reports (Nos. 52, 57), Marmaduke's report (No. 71) and the incomplete casualty return (No. 50) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam's, 1899) is a retrospective history described on its title page as based upon official reports and the author's observations; it gives figures from Union and Confederate reports and incomplete Confederate returns, so it is not independent of the Official Records families. Price's report dated Camden, May 1864 is one family of interested Confederate accounts. Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIV, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
